arguments.name: The root can disclose Himself
arguments.speaker: Author
arguments.conclusion: If God is the root, He is not confined to the far end of human investigation but can disclose Himself.
premises: P1 Human beings can reason upward from existence, truth, relation, order, consciousness, morality, beauty, suffering, and history to ask what kind of root could carry all of that.
P2 But if God is actually God, He is not trapped at the far end of our investigation.
P3 The root can disclose Himself.

st1.quote: But if God is actually God, He is not trapped at the far end of our investigation.

st2.quote: Human beings can reason upward. We can look at existence, truth, relation, order, consciousness, morality, beauty, suffering, and history.

st6.quote: But if God is actually God, He is not trapped at the far end of our investigation.

or1.quote: But if God is actually God, He is not trapped at the far end of our investigation.
or1.why: A variant on the classical claim that the transcendent ground can reveal itself; applied here as a framing move for the project.

or2.why: No new premise or data beyond the classical appeal to God's self-disclosure.

or3.why: No cross-domain bridge; it stays within theology/philosophy.

arguments.prior_art: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae (via eminentiae / divine self-disclosure), 1265-1274
arguments.weakest_link: P2 — the inference from 'God is God' to 'He is not trapped at the far end of our investigation' is asserted, not argued.
arguments.develop_next: State the premise explicitly as 'a self-existent personal ground cannot be exhaustively reached by finite inference' and defend it against the objection that a silent God is consistent with theism.

arguments.name: The divine name is a boundary, not a creaturely label
arguments.speaker: Author
arguments.conclusion: The name 'I AM WHO I AM' functions as a boundary that prevents God from being defined by comparison to created things.
premises: P1 Most names work by comparison, placing things among other things and noticing what separates them.
P2 But the One being named is not one object among others.
P3 You cannot define the root by pointing beneath it, because if something deeper explains God, then God was not the root.
P4 You cannot place God inside a category larger than God, because then the category would be more ultimate than God.
P5 Therefore the divine name refuses to let God be measured from below.

st2.quote: You cannot define the root by pointing beneath it. If something deeper explains God, then God was not the root.

st3.quote: Most names work by comparison. A tree is not a stone. A father is not a son.

st4.quote: So the divine name does something strange and necessary. It refuses to let God be measured from below.

st6.quote: The name does not answer every philosophical question. It does not hand us a diagram of God’s essence. It does not remove mystery.

st8.quote: You cannot define the root by pointing beneath it... You cannot place God inside a category larger than God.

or1.quote: It refuses to let God be measured from below.
or1.why: A restatement of the classical apophatic reading of Exodus 3:14, framed as a 'boundary' rather than an essence description.

or2.why: No new evidence or premise beyond the standard comparative-naming argument.

arguments.prior_art: Gregory of Nyssa / Pseudo-Dionysius, apophatic theology of the divine name, c. 390 / c. 500
arguments.weakest_link: P2 — 'the One being named is not one object among others' is assumed rather than established.
arguments.develop_next: Add a defence that the root cannot be a member of a larger category, engaging the objection that 'being' itself is the wider class.

arguments.name: Revelation is not cheating
arguments.speaker: Author
arguments.conclusion: It is not irrational to listen to a personal God who can speak, and revelation is a legitimate route to knowledge of Him.
premises: P1 If God speaks, then revelation is not cheating.
P2 It is not irrational to listen to a person who can speak.
P3 If God is personal, and if creation is not God, then creatures should not assume that their upward reasoning is the only possible route to knowledge of Him.
P4 A child can learn about his father both by studying the house the father built and by hearing his father speak.
P5 The house can witness to the father, and the father's voice can explain the house.

st1.quote: If God speaks, then revelation is not cheating.

st2.quote: It is not irrational to listen to a person who can speak.

st3.quote: A child can learn about his father in two ways. He can study the house the father built... But the child can also hear his father speak.

st4.quote: Those are not enemies. The house can witness to the father. The father’s voice can explain the house.

st6.quote: If God is personal, and if creation is not God, then creatures should not assume that their upward reasoning is the only possible route to knowledge of Him.

st8.quote: The house can witness to the father. The father’s voice can explain the house.

or1.quote: Science studies the house. Philosophy asks what the house requires. Scripture records the Father speaking.
or1.why: A variant of the two-books / twofold-knowledge tradition, applied to the project's method.

or2.why: No new data; the father/house analogy is traditional.

or3.quote: Science studies the house. Philosophy asks what the house requires. Scripture records the Father speaking.
or3.why: Loosely connects scientific, philosophical and scriptural methods, though without a technical bridge.

arguments.prior_art: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (duplex cognitio Domini), 1559
arguments.weakest_link: P1 — 'if God speaks, revelation is not cheating' only works against a caricature; it does not address how we identify genuine divine speech.
arguments.develop_next: Add a criterion for distinguishing genuine revelation from false claims, since S113 concedes claims of revelation can be false.

arguments.name: Jesus takes the divine name into Himself
arguments.speaker: Author
arguments.conclusion: Jesus's 'I am' declarations are identity language that press the root question into history, not ordinary religious advice.
premises: P1 In John's Gospel, Jesus repeatedly says 'I am' and attaches to Himself roles too large for a mere teacher.
P2 A prophet can say 'God gives bread,' but Jesus says 'I am the bread.'
P3 A teacher can say 'I will show you truth,' but Jesus says 'I am the truth.'
P4 A guide can say 'I know the way,' but Jesus says 'I am the way.'
P5 A comforter can say 'God will raise the dead,' but Jesus says 'I am the resurrection and the life.'
P6 That is not ordinary religious advice; it is identity language.

st1.quote: That is not ordinary religious advice. It is identity language.

st2.quote: A prophet can say, “God gives bread.” Jesus says, “I am the bread.”

st3.quote: In John’s Gospel, Jesus repeatedly says “I am” and then attaches to Himself roles too large for a mere teacher: “I am the bread of life.” ... “I am the true vine.”

st4.quote: Jesus does not merely speak about God from a distance. He identifies Himself in ways that press the root question into history.

st5.quote: It does not prove by itself that Jesus is who Christianity says He is. Anyone can make a large claim. The support layer must face the historical questions, the Johannine context, rival religious claims, translation issues, and resurrection evidence.

st6.quote: It does not prove by itself that Jesus is who Christianity says He is.

st7.quote: The support layer must face the historical questions, the Johannine context, rival religious claims, translation issues, and resurrection evidence.

st8.quote: A prophet can say, “God gives bread.” Jesus says, “I am the bread.” ... A guide can say, “I know the way.” Jesus says, “I am the way.”

or1.quote: That is not ordinary religious advice. It is identity language.
or1.why: The egō eimi identity reading is standard Johannine scholarship; here it is repackaged as pressing the 'root question' into history.

or2.why: Uses the same Johannine texts as prior work, with no new evidence.

or3.quote: He identifies Himself in ways that press the root question into history.
or3.why: Connects the Johannine sayings to the project's root/ground framework.

arguments.prior_art: Raymond E. Brown, The Gospel According to John (egō eimi sayings), 1966-1970
arguments.weakest_link: The inference from the 'I am' sayings to a claim about the divine name (Exodus 3:14) depends on an identification the text does not explicitly make.
arguments.develop_next: Argue the linguistic link between the Johannine egō eimi and the LXX of Exodus 3:14, and address the objection that 'I am the bread' is a predicate nominative rather than a divine-name claim.

arguments.name: Christianity is built on disclosure, not only inference
arguments.speaker: Author
arguments.conclusion: Christianity is not built only on upward inference but on God's disclosure of Himself.
premises: P1 If God remains only an inference, then every argument about God stays trapped inside creaturely reach.
P2 We can argue from effects to cause, from order to source, from morality to ground, from consciousness to personhood, from beauty to meaning.
P3 Those arguments may matter, some may be strong, some may fail, some may only point.
P4 But Christianity is not built only on upward inference; it is built on disclosure.
P5 God speaks, acts, covenants, comes, names Himself, reveals His character, and enters the human story in Christ.

st1.quote: But Christianity is not built only on upward inference. It is built on disclosure.

st2.quote: We can argue from effects to cause, from order to source, from morality to ground, from consciousness to personhood, from beauty to meaning.

st3.quote: God speaks. God acts. God covenants. God comes. God names Himself. God reveals His character. God enters the human story in Christ.

st4.quote: If God remains only an inference, then every argument about God stays trapped inside creaturely reach.

st6.quote: Those arguments may matter. Some may be strong. Some may fail. Some may only point.

st8.quote: We can argue from effects to cause, from order to source, from morality to ground, from consciousness to personhood, from beauty to meaning.

or1.quote: But Christianity is not built only on upward inference. It is built on disclosure.
or1.why: A variant of the revelation-priority tradition, stated as a methodological posture rather than a full Barthian argument.

or3.quote: Science studies the house. Philosophy asks what the house requires. Scripture records the Father speaking.

arguments.prior_art: Karl Barth, Church Dogmatics (revelation over natural theology), 1932-1967
arguments.weakest_link: P4 — the 'not only... but' claim is asserted; it does not show that disclosure is needed, only that it is claimed.
arguments.develop_next: Give an argument that inferential routes are structurally insufficient (not merely incomplete), otherwise the 'only' is doing rhetorical work.

arguments.name: Revelation does not remove the need for argument
arguments.speaker: Author
arguments.conclusion: Even if God has spoken, argument, interpretation, and investigation remain necessary.
premises: P1 Revelation can be misunderstood.
P2 Claims of revelation can be false.
P3 Scripture must be interpreted.
P4 History must be investigated.
P5 The Church can mishandle what it receives.
P6 Therefore revelation does not remove the need for argument.

st1.quote: That does not remove the need for argument.

st2.quote: Revelation can be misunderstood. Claims of revelation can be false. Scripture must be interpreted. History must be investigated. The Church can mishandle what it receives.

st3.quote: Claims of revelation can be false.

st4.quote: But if God has spoken, then the highest form of knowledge is not guessing correctly about a silent source.

st6.quote: That does not remove the need for argument.

st8.quote: Revelation can be misunderstood. Claims of revelation can be false.

or1.quote: Scripture must be interpreted. History must be investigated.
or1.why: A variant of the standard hermeneutical point that revelation requires interpretation.

arguments.weakest_link: The move from 'revelation can be misunderstood' to 'argument remains necessary' does not specify what kind of argument or how much.
arguments.develop_next: Specify the method (e.g. historical-critical and hermeneutical criteria) by which revelation claims are tested, so the claim becomes operational.

arguments.name: The paper's claim is conditional, not a proof of God's existence
arguments.speaker: Author
arguments.conclusion: The paper is not arguing 'Exodus 3:14 is in the Bible, therefore God exists,' but rather describing the kind of God Christianity identifies.
premises: P1 A skeptic does not have to accept the Bible's authority to understand what this paper is doing.
P2 The paper is not saying 'Exodus 3:14 is in the Bible, therefore God exists.'
P3 It is saying 'If Christianity is being treated as testimony, this is the kind of God it identifies: self-existent, non-derived, personal, speaking, faithful, and finally revealed in Christ.'
P4 The disclosed portrait can be stated honestly before it is proven publicly.
P5 We can ask what Christianity claims, then ask whether reality, reason, history, and experience converge with that claim.

st1.quote: This paper is not saying: “Exodus 3:14 is in the Bible, therefore God exists.”

st2.quote: It is saying: “If Christianity is being treated as testimony, this is the kind of God it identifies: self-existent, non-derived, personal, speaking, faithful, and finally revealed in Christ.”

st3.quote: The disclosed portrait can be stated honestly before it is proven publicly. We can ask what Christianity claims. Then we can ask whether reality, reason, history, and experience converge with that claim.

st6.quote: A skeptic does not have to accept the Bible’s authority to understand what this paper is doing.

st7.quote: Then we can ask whether reality, reason, history, and experience converge with that claim.

st8.quote: Then we can ask whether reality, reason, history, and experience converge with that claim.

or1.quote: This paper is not saying: “Exodus 3:14 is in the Bible, therefore God exists.”
or1.why: A methodological clarification rather than a restatement of a prior argument; it defines the paper's dialectical status.

or2.quote: We can ask what Christianity claims. Then we can ask whether reality, reason, history, and experience converge with that claim.
or2.why: No new evidence; it is a scope statement.

arguments.weakest_link: P4 — 'can be stated honestly before it is proven publicly' risks insulating the portrait from falsification.
arguments.develop_next: State explicitly what would count as the portrait failing to converge with reality, reason, history and experience.

arguments.name: The I AM declarations prevent reductionism
arguments.speaker: Author
arguments.conclusion: The 'I AM' declarations keep us from reducing God to an object at the end of an argument and from reducing Jesus to a moral teacher.
premises: P1 The 'I AM' declarations belong here because they keep us from reducing God to an object at the end of an argument.
P2 They also keep us from reducing Jesus to a moral teacher with unusually devoted followers.
P3 The Bible's claim is far larger: the root is not silent, the root speaks, and in Christ the root walks into the room.

st1.quote: They keep us from reducing God to an object at the end of an argument.

st2.quote: They also keep us from reducing Jesus to a moral teacher with unusually devoted followers.

st4.quote: The root is not silent. The root speaks. And in Christ, Christianity says, the root walks into the room.

st6.quote: The Bible’s claim is far larger.

or1.quote: They also keep us from reducing Jesus to a moral teacher with unusually devoted followers.
or1.why: A variant of the Lewis trilemma, restated as a guard against reductionism rather than a formal dilemma.

arguments.weakest_link: P1/P2 — the claim that the declarations 'keep us from' reductionism is asserted without showing the mechanism.
arguments.develop_next: Show how the identity language entails a unique ontological claim that moral-teacher readings cannot accommodate, rather than merely asserting it.
